en: I shall explain the procedure for the water-oblation (*jalahoma*), which has come down through the lineage of the four seats (*catuṣpīṭha*);
by means of this ritual of oblation, rites such as pacification (*śāntika*) and others are accomplished. [7.1]

One should construct a square mandala measuring four cubits, smeared with fragrant cow dung; there, one should hang a brilliantly shining canopy. And on all sides, eight banners of various brilliant colors [should be placed].
The vessel should have a mouth fourteen finger-breadths wide and be adorned with auspicious marks;
it should be nine finger-breadths deep, bright white, and like a *śānti* hearth,
its great belly filled with pure milk and water free from insects.
Having established eight vessels and likewise others in the center of the mandala, one should place similar auspicious vessels filled with scented water in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
these should be adorned with mango sprouts and their necks decorated with fine cloth.
Having instantly formed the visualization joined with the Jñāna-Ḍākinī,
and having made the two hands into the shape of a lotus with the lotus-mudrā,
one should recite the mantra and display the mudrā over the vessel.
Oṃ kamalābhe svāhā.
In the midst of water there is a lotus; upon the lotus is the moon;
on the moon is the seed-syllable *HŪṂ*, and that seed-syllable is Jñānaḍākinī.
She sits in the sattva-paryaṅka posture, wrathful, and faces with laughter and the erotic sentiment.
Furthermore, she holds with her two hands a pair of white staffs marked with vajras at their upper ends; endowed with a mandala,
she emanates from her own body a Wisdom Being (jñānasattvī) who is identical to herself.
[One should visualize her] as two-armed and three-faced, white in color, and bearing the same colors and implements [as the deity].
Having caused her to enter the visualized water-deity, one should worship her again with the *argha* and other offerings;
then, having worshipped her with white flowers, one should display the mudrā.
Having formed the hands into fists with the backs joined together,
one should extend the pair of index fingers and form a knot with them;
this is to be known as the Samaya-mudrā, and its mantra is now being told.
Oṃ samaya tiṣṭha hūṃ!
In the previously mentioned eastern vessel are Ḍākinī and Ghorī;
Vetālī is on the western side, and Caṇḍālī is situated in the south. [7.14]
Siṃhī is in the northeastern compartments; Vyāghrī is in the southeast, while Jambukī is to be known in the southwestern corner, and Ulūkī is considered to be in the northwest.
They should be visualized as having arisen from their own seed-syllables and bearing emblems such as swords and the like.
All of them are situated upon a moon on a lotus, established by their own inherent nature.
Alternatively, the respective insignia should be specifically drawn as resting upon a lotus and moon;
one should cause the sword of Vajraḍākinī to be drawn, radiating with light.
The hook made of rays belongs to Ghorāḍākinī, while the battle-axe belongs to Vetālī;
the bright vajra-staff belongs to Caṇḍālī—such is the sign in every respect. [7.18]
One should indicate that for all the goddesses of the corners beginning with Śivā, there is a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) blazing with vajras, situated in the center of a universal lotus;
likewise, there is the procedure for entry and so forth, consisting of such Knowledge Beings (jñānasattva).
One should display the root mudrā preceded by the recitation of the mantra.
Having placed the left fist at the heart, one should then place the right [fist] above it;
this is to be known as the root mudrā, which one should display for the yoginīs. [7.20–7.21]
Oṃ jrūṃ jrūṃ svāhā.
The preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is performed over the period of three hundred thousand recitations;

one should also offer white flowers and the like into the sacrificial fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) by means of this very [mantra]. Furthermore, at the base of each flower, one should cast *dūrvā* grass and perform the oblation (*homayet*).
Having meditated on the water as the crown of the Ḍākinī, one should strike it again.
[7.23] Having recited each mantra once, one should cast a flower into the water.
One should offer as an oblation a red karavīra flower and *pūrvaga* (or *puṃnāga*) and *nāgakesara*; by means of that, one accomplishes every purpose.
The specific distinction for all [rites] through the *ayuta*-homa is also stated here:
as before, if one offers one hundred and eight handfuls of water daily to the Crowned Jñānaḍākinī, [the result follows].
There is an increase of wealth and growth, and prosperity occurs; it is not otherwise.

One who knows the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as being without intrinsic nature, free from all distinctions, and unattached, should perform the fire offering (*homa*) through the application of mudrās, mantras, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), being a perfected practitioner.
Or alternatively:
One whose self is the yoga of one's chosen deity, peaceful and capable in the rite of pacification,
having prepared the vessel as before, filled with substances such as sugar and the like,
and having properly generated Vajrasattva within one’s own heart—
Seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, with two arms and holding a vajra;
holding a bell in the left hand, peaceful, and merged with the Jñānasattva.
However, in the eight vessels in the cardinal directions, from the center of a universal lotus and moon disk:
The skillful practitioner should visualize the signs, beginning with the eternal Tārā;
furthermore, he should perform everything else as before, such as the offering of water (argha) and the fire-oblation (homa).
At that time, the one to be accomplished (sādhya) should also be visualized as peaceful and clad in white garments.
Adorned with various ornaments and seated upon a jeweled throne and the like, his mind filled with joy, he possesses a parasol; indeed, wise and pure, he has bathed in nectar.
By the light of the seed-syllable in his heart, he draws forth the assembly of deities beginning with Locanā.

Then, by means of a continuous rain from jars filled with nectar falling upon his limbs, he becomes clear and freed from all bodily impurities. By such a procedure, one whose life is exhausted or who is afflicted by disease [is restored].
Through the practice of this yoga for six months, a person becomes long-lived. [7.35] This is the water-oblation (jalahoma).
